title: ReNU SYNDROME
alt_titles: NEURODEVELOPMENTAL DISORDER WITH HYPOTONIA, BRAIN ANOMALIES, DISTINCTIVE FACIES, AND ABSENT LANGUAGE

intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that ReNU syndrome (RENU) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the RNU4-2 gene (620823) on chromosome 12q24.31.

checks.claim: ReNU syndrome (RENU) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the RNU4-2 gene.
checks.evidence_quote: We identify an 18 base pair region of RNU4-2 mapping to two structural elements in the U4/U6 snRNA duplex (the T-loop and stem III) that is severely depleted of variation in the general population, but in which we identify heterozygous variants in 115 individuals with NDD.

paragraphs.text: ReNU syndrome is a neurodevelopmental disorder. Chen et al. (2024) found moderate to severe global developmental delay and intellectual disability in all affected individuals. Other features were delayed ambulation, speech that was mostly absent, microcephaly, short stature, hypotonia, seizures, abnormalities on brain MRI, and distinctive facial features.

paragraphs.text: Greene et al. (2024) studied 47 unrelated cases from the UK 100,000 Genomes Project who carried rare RNU4-2 variants in 2 regions, n.62-70 and n.73-79. Forty-six of them were coded with neurodevelopmental abnormality. Among these 46, 91% had intellectual disability, 91% had neurodevelopmental delay, and 61% had motor delay, which was broadly in line with term frequencies across all intellectual disability cases. Several features were more frequent than in other cases coded with neurodevelopmental abnormality: microcephaly in 57% (vs 18%), drooling in 13% (vs 1%), proportionate short stature in 28% (vs 7%), and generalized hypotonia in 39% (vs 13%). Seizures were present in 52%, and 6 of the 46 had an abnormality of the upper lip vermilion.

paragraphs.text: Chen et al. (2024) collected detailed phenotypic data on 49 individuals (21 female and 28 male) with variants in the RNU4-2 critical region. Their median age was 10 years (range, 2 to 38 years). All 49 had global developmental delay, which was severe in 34. All 45 who were assessed had intellectual disability. Walking was delayed, and 7 of 30 had an abnormal gait. Forty-five of 48 had a speech abnormality, and 35 of 45 were nonverbal. Behavioral issues were reported in 30 of 45, autism spectrum disorder in 21 of 44, and sleep issues in 15 of 32. Thirty-nine of 45 had hypotonia, and 37 of 48 had seizures. Brain MRI was abnormal in 41 of 45; findings included reduced white matter volume, hypoplasia of the corpus callosum, ventriculomegaly, and delayed myelination. Growth was affected in many patients: intrauterine growth restriction in 8 of 45, short stature in 37 of 49, microcephaly in 37 of 48 (congenital in 19 of 37), and growth problems in 30 of 43. Hearing loss was found in 10 of 46. Thirty-eight of 48 had vision issues, including optic nerve hypoplasia (8 of 37), strabismus (23 of 45), nystagmus (18 of 40), and cortical blindness. Gastrointestinal problems included constipation (29 of 44), gastroesophageal reflux (21 of 43), and feeding difficulties (32 of 42); 13 of 41 were fed by gastrostomy tube. Other abnormalities were endocrine (17 of 39), bone or skeletal, including osteopenia and scoliosis (27 of 42), limb (23 of 42), genitourinary (15 of 43), dental (17 of 43), cardiac (5 of 43), and cutaneous (25 of 44). Forty-five of 48 had dysmorphic facial features, among them deep-set eyes, epicanthus, wide nasal bridge, anteverted nares, large cupped ears, full cheeks, downturned corners of the mouth, high-arched palate, and a large or protruding tongue.

paragraphs.text: Most cases of ReNU syndrome are caused by de novo heterozygous mutations, and the disorder shows autosomal dominant transmission. Greene et al. (2024) reported the following inheritance data: - In their discovery set, 37 of 47 variants were de novo, and inheritance was unknown for the remaining 10. - The mother of 1 proband was mosaic for an n.65A-G variant. - Among the replication probands, 19 of 26 affected probands had de novo variants, and inheritance was unknown for 6. - One proband inherited n.76C-T from an affected mother. Chen et al. (2024) reported the following: - An n.77_78insT variant was present in 2 affected sibs. - In 1 individual, the n.65A-G variant appeared to be mosaic in the mother. - In another individual, n.76C-T was maternally inherited.

paragraphs.text: Greene et al. (2024) identified RNU4-2 through a burden analysis of 100,000 Genomes Project data. The disease-associated heterozygous variants clustered in 2 contiguous regions, n.62-70 and n.73-79. No unaffected participant carried a rare variant in either region, and the locus as a whole was depleted of variation in gnomAD. Of 47 rare variants in 47 cases, 37 were de novo. The most common variant, n.64_65insT, arose de novo in 33 different families. Other variants included n.63T-G, n.64_65insG, n.65A-G, n.65_66insT, n.67A-G, n.68_69insA, n.76C-T, and n.77_78insT. Replication in 3 further collections brought the total to 73 unrelated cases.

Most variants were de novo. The n.64_65insT variant arose de novo in 38 Genomics England probands. It was absent from 3,408 diagnosed probands with neurodevelopmental disorders, 21,817 probands without neurodevelopmental disorders, 33,122 unaffected individuals, gnomAD v4.0, and All of Us. Single-base insertions in the critical region were strongly enriched in undiagnosed probands with neurodevelopmental disorders compared with UK Biobank (odds ratio, 1,531). In the 54 individuals in whom parental origin could be determined, all de novo variants were on the maternal allele.

paragraphs.text: Chen et al. (2024) noted that the 18-bp critical region maps to the T-loop (quasi-pseudoknot) and stem III of the U4/U6 duplex. These structures are loaded into the BRR2 helicase and are thought to stabilize U4/U6 pairing and to position the U6 ACAGAGA sequence to receive the 5-prime splice site. In human prefrontal cortex, RNU4-2 was consistently expressed at higher levels than its homolog RNU4-1 throughout development, and it showed greater chromatin accessibility in prenatal cortex; these findings supported RNU4-2 as the main U4 transcript in the brain. Blood RNA-seq in 5 individuals with RNU4-2 variants showed increased use of unannotated 5-prime splice sites compared with controls. At these sites, the bases at positions +3, +4, and +5, which pair with U6 ACAGAGA, shifted away from the consensus. The authors concluded that the variants disrupt accurate recognition of the 5-prime splice site during spliceosome activation.
